videos.script: Every week a system has fixes waiting. Most are for security flaws somebody found and published, which means that from the day a fix appears, the flaw is public and every machine without it is a known target. {{fixes}} And every so often an update breaks something. The old scanner at reception stops scanning after a Windows feature update, because its driver was written years ago and nobody has written a new one. So updating is not a yes or a no; it is how soon, to which machines, and with a way back. {{scanner}} Drivers are the part of this that most often goes wrong, because they come from the most places: some with the system, some through its updates, and some from whoever made the device. {{drivers}} In this lesson you will read what an update actually contains, turn on automatic security updates on the server, hold back a package that must not change, decide how fast each kind of update should arrive, find where a driver came from, and understand why a program built for one system or one version refuses to run on another. {{steps}} The Linux transcripts come from lesson 3's server. The Windows and Mac commands are shown, not run. {{honest}}
